purpose: Review a more recent native-range river-system study of weather-loach diet, retaining the July stomach-content subset, size effects, sympatry context, and taxonomic limits.

study.title: Occurrence Patterns and Food Habits of Introduced Alien Loach Paramisgurnus dabryanus and Native Loach Misgurnus anguillicaudatus at Irrigation Drainages around Rice Fields in the Watarase River System, Central Honshu, Japan
study.citation: Kanou, K., Saito, S., Fuchigami, S., Imamura, A., Imai, H., & Taki, Y. (2007). Aquaculture Science, 55(1), 109-114. https://doi.org/10.11233/aquaculturesci1953.55.109.
study.researchPeriodAsReported: Occurrence sampling from January 2005 through January 2006; gut-content analysis of co-occurring fish collected in July 2005.
study.studyLocation: Irrigation drainages around rice fields in the Watarase River system, central Honshu, Japan.
methodsAsReported: The authors sampled multiple irrigation-drainage reaches around rice fields through the annual survey and report hand-net collection effort for defined channel reaches.
For diet analysis, stomach contents from the July co-occurrence sample were measured using percentage volume, percentage frequency, and a vacuity index.

The study distinguished the native M. anguillicaudatus from co-occurring introduced Paramisgurnus dabryanus using reported morphological characteristics. The reviewed article does not provide specimen accession or molecular confirmation records.

findingsAsReported.sizePattern: Both loaches mainly ate ostracods below 30 mm standard length; larger individuals shifted toward insect larvae and/or Branchinella kugenumaensis.
findingsAsReported.cooccurringSpeciesContext: The paper reports high stomach-content overlap between same-size classes of M. anguillicaudatus and P. dabryanus during their July sympatry. This describes resource overlap; it is not evidence that either loach ate the other fish.

evidenceLimits: The overall 3023 M. anguillicaudatus were occurrence-survey captures across the study period; only 121 stomachs from the July co-occurrence period were examined for diet. Do not describe the diet sample as year-round.
This is a Japanese native-range rice-field drainage study, not a Philippine river, lake, or fishery sample.
Species identification was based on reported morphology in a setting with a similar non-native loach; no voucher accession or molecular confirmation was reported in the reviewed article.

The prey evidence is limited to sampled size classes, one July co-occurrence period, and one river-system setting. It does not prove every prey item is eaten in other seasons, habitats, life stages, or regions.

The study does not report fish prey in the summarized major foods and does not support claims that this species naturally eats conspecific fish, nor does it support bait, catchability, or legal guidance.
J-STAGE provides the article as a free journal item; no item-specific redistribution license was verified. No PDF tables or data were copied into Bangwit.

relationshipToOtherDietEvidence.assessment: This 2005-2006 Japan study directly reports stomach contents by size in a rice-field drainage system and complements Kubota's older Nagata River study. The studies differ in locality, season, method and life-stage coverage; neither establishes Philippine diet.

nextAction: Seek Philippine diet observations tied to confidently identified specimens and named waterbodies/seasons. Until then, any diet presentation should state source locality, sample method, size and season, and remain distinct from bait advice.

sources.supports: Journal metadata, sampling period, overall and diet-subset counts, stomach-content method, prey taxa, body-size pattern, and co-occurring loach context.
